hook.text: Early railways couldn't agree on how wide the tracks should be. Decades of chaos followed.

buildup.text: Stephenson chose 4 feet 8.5 inches. Brunel preferred 7 feet, arguing wider meant smoother.

discovery.text: Where different gauges met, passengers and cargo had to switch trains. Slow and expensive.

twist.text: Parliament forced a national standard in 1846. Brunel's wider gauge was better but lost.

climax.text: The Great Western Railway ripped up thousands of miles of broad-gauge track to comply.

quiz.question: Why did Brunel's broad gauge lose the Gauge Wars?
options: Parliament chose the narrower standard for compatibility
